content: Astroviruses are a group of viruses that infect humans. They have been relatively understudied because they do not grow well in laboratory culture systems. These viruses belong to the family Astroviridae, which also includes mamastroviruses. Astroviruses were first identified in 1975 during an outbreak of diarrhea, using electron microscopy. Structurally, astroviruses have a non-segmented, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome enclosed within a non-enveloped, icosahedral capsid. Astroviruses are now recognized as a significant cause of gastroenteritis in both children and adults. These viruses are non-enveloped and exhibit cubic symmetry, with a diameter of approximately 28-30 nanometers. Their genome is composed of a positive-sense single strand of RNA that encodes various structural proteins. A study conducted in the United Kingdom in 1999 reported an incidence rate of 3.8 cases per 1,000 patient-years in the community, making astroviruses the fourth most common known cause of viral gastroenteritis. In the United States, astroviruses have been detected in the stool samples of 2-9% of children presenting with symptoms of gastroenteritis. The illness is most frequently observed in children under the age of two, although outbreaks have also been documented among adults and the elderly. Early research conducted in Glasgow revealed that 12% of infants shedding astrovirus particles in their stool did not exhibit any gastrointestinal symptoms. Additionally, seroprevalence studies in the United States have shown that by the age of nine, 90% of children have antibodies against human astrovirus serotype 1 (HastV-1), indicating that asymptomatic infections are common. Similar to other viral causes of gastroenteritis, astrovirus infections tend to peak during the winter months. The clinical symptoms of astrovirus infection include diarrhea, headache, malaise, and nausea. Vomiting is less commonly reported. The symptoms are generally milder compared to those caused by rotavirus infections, and dehydration is less severe as a result. The incubation period for astrovirus infection is typically 3-4 days, and symptoms usually resolve within five days in uncomplicated cases. Diagnosis of astrovirus infection can be achieved through electron microscopy, as the virus is present in large quantities in stool samples, making immune amplification unnecessary. Other diagnostic methods include enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), immunofluorescence, and nucleic acid-based techniques. Treatment is often not required, but oral rehydration therapy can be used to maintain electrolyte balance. There is potential for the development of a vaccine, as infection appears to provide short-term immunity against viruses of the same serotype. When diagnosing astrovirus infection, it is important to differentiate it from other causes of viral, bacterial, and parasitic gastroenteritis. Small bowel diarrhea, which is watery and voluminous with fewer than five white blood cells per high-power field, differs from large bowel diarrhea, which is mucousy and/or bloody, with smaller volume and more than ten white blood cells per high-power field. The severity of diarrhea and the immune status of the patient can influence the clinical presentation, with white blood cell counts potentially reaching as high as 1,000 in some cases.
